core.text: A few everyday adjectives change their whole stem when compared: **the irregular comparatives and superlatives (better / best, worse / worst, bigger / biggest)**. *bonus* (good) → *melior, melius* → *optimus*; *malus* (bad) → *peior, peius* → *pessimus*; *magnus* (big) → *māior, māius* → *maximus*; *parvus* (small) → *minor, minus* → *minimus*; *multī* (many) → *plūrēs, plūra* → *plūrimī*; and *multum* (much) → *plūs* → *plūrimum*. Latin name: comparātiō anomala.
*Good, better, best* and *bad, worse, worst* are English irregular comparisons — the *-er* form is a different word. Latin's list is nearly the same.
melior / optimus, peior / pessimus, māior / maximus, minor / minimus, plūrēs / plūrimī: new stems, regular endings.

invented.la: Hic liber melior est quam ille.
invented.en: This book is better than that one.

core.text: *māior* and *longior* work exactly alike — both are the comparative (the '-er / more' form), both take *quam* (than) and 3rd-declension endings. The trap is spotting them: *melior* has no *bonus* inside it, so learn the pairs as vocabulary. *minus* and *plūs* also serve as adverbs and nouns: *minus pulchra* — less beautiful; *plūs dīcere* — to say more.

more.text: Only the stems are strange: the comparatives decline like any *-ior* word (*meliōrem*), the superlatives like *bonus -a -um*. *plūs* in the singular is a neuter noun with a genitive after it: *plūs pecūniae* — more money; only the plural *plūrēs, plūra* agrees like an adjective. Related sets: *superus* → *superior* → *suprēmus / summus*; *īnferus* → *īnferior* → *īnfimus / īmus*; *senex* (old) → *senior*; *iuvenis* (young) → *iūnior*.

*māior* and *minor* also mean *older* and *younger*: Quintus is *māior est quam Iūlia* — older than Julia; *maximus / minimus līberōrum* — the eldest / youngest of the children. *optimus* is the everyday word for *excellent*.

The learner's notes (week 19): a handful of adjectives in both languages form their comparative and superlative from very different stems — *bonus / melior / optimus*, *malus / peior / pessimus*, *magnus / māior / maximus*, *parvus / minor / minimus*, *multus / plūs (plūrēs) / plūrimus* — and apart from the stems they act normally. Ørberg (chapter XIX margin): *multum, comp. plūs, sup. plūrimum; paulum, comp. minus, sup. minimum*; A&G §129 give the full list.

teach.title: What these words do
teach.say: Most adjectives compare by adding to their own stem, but a few of the commonest change word altogether: the irregular comparatives and superlatives (better / best, worse / worst, bigger / biggest). *Bonus* 'good' gives *melior* 'better' and *optimus* 'best' — a different word at each step, with nothing of *bonus* left in it. English does exactly the same thing in good, better, best, so the idea is already familiar; only the Latin words are new.

check.ask: Tap the word that compares Quintus with Julia.

teach.title: The comparative: a new stem, the ending -ior / -ius
teach.say: The comparative (the '-er / more' form) keeps its ordinary ending and puts it on the new stem. *Bonus* does not build on *bon-* at all: its comparative stem is *meli-*, and *meli-* + *-or* gives *melior*. The other stems are *pēi-* from *malus*, *min-* from *parvus*, *māi-* from *magnus*. For a neuter word the ending is *-ius* instead of *-or*: *melior* beside *melius*. The word for 'than' after any of them is *quam*.

show.say: melior, melius — the new stem, then -or or -ius

check.ask: Now build the same two cells on magnus: the comparative, masculine and neuter.

teach.title: The superlative: a new stem, the ordinary -us -a -um
teach.say: The superlative (the '-est / most' form) is just as regular once the stem is right. *Bonus* has the superlative stem *opti-*, so *optimus, optima, optimum*; *parvus* has *mini-*, *magnus* has *māxi-*. They take the plain first-and-second-declension endings (the ordinary *-us -a -um* set; a declension is which family of endings a noun or adjective takes), so they agree with their noun exactly as *bonus* does — masculine *-us*, feminine *-a*, neuter *-um*.

show.say: optimus, optima — the superlative stem with the ordinary endings

check.ask: Now build the same two cells on magnus: the superlative, masculine and feminine.

teach.title: multī, plūrēs, plūrimī — and plūs
teach.say: *Multī* 'many' compares to *plūrēs* 'more (in number)' and *plūrimī* 'very many'. In the singular the comparative is not an adjective at all but the noun *plūs* 'more', which takes the genitive (the 'of' form) after it: *plūs pecūniae*, more money. So *plūs* weighs an amount and stands alone, while the plural counts things you could number one by one and agrees with them like any adjective.

check.ask: plūrēs — which noun does it agree with, and how do you know it is not plūs?

teach.title: Telling it from the regular comparative
teach.say: Both kinds end the same way, so look at the stem and not at the ending. *Longus* gives *longior* — the adjective is still there inside it, and you could put the word back together. *Parvus* gives *minor* — the adjective has gone. If you can still see the word you started from, the comparison is regular; if you cannot, it belongs to this short list.

check.ask: Tap the comparative whose stem is no longer the adjective it comes from.

teach.title: Using it
teach.say: The same irregular pairs work as adverbs too — *bene* 'well' gives *melius* 'better', *male* 'badly' gives *pēius* 'worse' — and there they lose their case endings altogether, as the sentence in front of you shows. But an adjective is what you build here, and it still agrees with its noun like any other: decide first what is being compared and what gender that word is, then write the form that fits it.
